# Overview

This in-class exercise uses the 88 counties of Hunan to measure spatial autocorrelation of GDP per capita with the **sfdep** package, first globally for the whole province and then locally for each county.

**sfdep** gives an sf and tidyverse friendly interface to **spdep**, and adds some functions that spdep does not have. It keeps neighbours, weights and results as list columns inside the sf data frame.

# Loading the Packages

Four packages are used, **sf**, **sfdep**, **tmap** and **tidyverse**.

```{r}
#| output: false
pacman::p_load(sf, sfdep, tmap, tidyverse)
```

# Preparing the Data

::: panel-tabset
## Importing Hunan shapefile

`st_read()` of **sf** reads the county boundaries into an sf polygon object.

```{r}
hunan <- st_read(dsn = "data/geospatial",
                 layer = "Hunan")
```

## Importing Hunan_2012 table

`read_csv()` of **readr** reads the 2012 indicators into a tibble.

```{r}
hunan2012 <- read_csv("data/aspatial/Hunan_2012.csv")
```
:::

# Combining Both Data Frames by Using Left Join

`left_join()` of **dplyr** attaches the 2012 indicators to the county polygons by the shared `County` column. `select()` keeps columns 1 to 4, 7, 15 and 33.

```{r}
hunan_GDPPC <- left_join(hunan, hunan2012) %>%
  select(1:4, 7, 15, 33)
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning diary
`hunan` has to be on the left of the join. The left data frame decides the type of the result, so putting the sf object first keeps the geometry and the output stays an sf data frame.
:::

# Plotting a Choropleth Map

`tm_shape()` and `tm_polygons()` of **tmap** map GDPPC with quantile classes, with a compass, scale bar and grid added.

::: panel-tabset
## The Plot

```{r}
#| echo: false
tmap_mode("plot")
tm_shape(hunan_GDPPC) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "GDPPC",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                values = "brewer.blues")) +
  tm_title("Distribution of GDP per capita by county, Hunan Province") +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_compass(type="8star", size = 2) +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_grid(fill_alpha =0.2) +
  tm_layout(legend.position = c("left", "bottom"))
```

## The Code

```{r}
#| eval: false
tmap_mode("plot")
tm_shape(hunan_GDPPC) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "GDPPC",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                values = "brewer.blues")) +
  tm_title("Distribution of GDP per capita by county, Hunan Province") +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
```

# Global Measures of Spatial Association

## Deriving Queen's Contiguity Weights with sfdep

`st_contiguity()` of **sfdep** builds the Queen neighbour list, and `st_weights()` turns it into weights. Both go into `hunan_GDPPC` as new columns, and `.before = 1` puts them at the front.

```{r}
wm_q <- hunan_GDPPC %>%
  mutate(nb = st_contiguity(geometry),
         wt = st_weights(nb,
                         style = "W"),
         .before = 1)
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning diary
`st_weights()` takes three inputs. `nb` is the neighbour list from `st_contiguity()`. `style` sets the weighting, and the default `"W"` row-standardises so each county's weights sum to 1. The other options are `"B"` binary, `"C"` globally standardised, `"U"` which is C divided by the number of neighbours, `"minmax"`, and `"S"` the variance-stabilising scheme of Tiefelsdorf et al. (1999). `allow_zero = TRUE` gives a lagged value of zero to a county with no neighbours. It is good practice to look at the output table after computing it.
:::

## Computing Global Moran's I

`global_moran()` of **sfdep** computes Moran's I. Unlike **spdep**, it returns its result as an object I can inspect with `glimpse()`, rather than a printed test report.

```{r}
moranI <- global_moran(wm_q$GDPPC,
                       wm_q$nb,
                       wm_q$wt)
glimpse(moranI)
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning diary
`I` is Moran's I, `r round(moranI$I, 3)`, the same value `moran.test()` gave in Hands-on Exercise 5. `K` is the sample kurtosis of GDPPC, `r round(moranI$K, 2)`. That is well above 3, the value for a normal distribution, so GDPPC has heavy tails. This function only computes the statistic. It does not test it, so there is no p-value here yet.
:::

## Performing Global Moran's I Test

In general, Moran's I is tested rather than just computed. `global_moran_test()` of **sfdep** runs the test.

::: panel-tabset
## The Code

```{r}
#| eval: false
global_moran_test(wm_q$GDPPC,
                       wm_q$nb,
                       wm_q$wt)
```

## The Output

```{r}
#| echo: false
moran_test <- global_moran_test(wm_q$GDPPC,
                       wm_q$nb,
                       wm_q$wt)
moran_test
```
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning diary
The `alternative` argument can be `"two.sided"`, `"greater"` or `"less"`. `randomization = TRUE` is the default. Setting it to `FALSE` assumes normality instead. The test gives a p-value of `r format.pval(moran_test$p.value, digits = 3)`, so the clustering of GDPPC is significant.
:::

## Performing Global Moran's I Permutation Test

In practice, Monte Carlo simulation should be used to test Moran's I. `global_moran_perm()` of **sfdep** shuffles GDPPC across the counties `nsim` times and compares the real Moran's I with the shuffled ones.

::: panel-tabset
## The Code

```{r}
#| eval: false
set.seed(1234)

global_moran_perm(wm_q$GDPPC,
                       wm_q$nb,
                       wm_q$wt,
                  nsim = 99)
```

## The Report

```{r}
#| echo: false
set.seed(1234)

global_moran_perm(wm_q$GDPPC,
                       wm_q$nb,
                       wm_q$wt,
                  nsim = 99)
```
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning diary
It is good practice to call `set.seed()` before any simulation, so the result can be reproduced. The number of simulations is always `nsim` + 1, so `nsim = 99` gives 100.

The p-value is below 0.05, so I reject the null hypothesis that GDPPC is spread at random across the counties. Moran's I is above 0, which means positive autocorrelation. Counties with high GDP per capita sit next to other high counties, and low next to low.
:::

# Local Measures of Spatial Association

## Computing Local Moran's I

`local_moran()` of **sfdep** computes local Moran's I of GDPPC for every county and tests each one with 99 simulations. It returns a data frame for each county, and `unnest()` of **tidyr** spreads it into ordinary columns.

::: panel-tabset
## The Code

```{r}
#| eval: false
lisa <- wm_q %>%
  mutate(local_moran = local_moran(
    GDPPC, nb, wt, nsim = 99),
         .before = 1) %>%
  unnest(local_moran)
```

## The Output

```{r}
#| echo: false
set.seed(1234)
lisa <- wm_q %>%
  mutate(local_moran = local_moran(
    GDPPC, nb, wt, nsim = 99),
         .before = 1) %>%
  unnest(local_moran)

glimpse(lisa)
```
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning diary
The main columns are `ii` (local Moran's I), `eii` (its expected value), `var_ii` (its variance), `z_ii` (the standard deviate), `p_ii` (the p-value from the normal approximation), `p_ii_sim` (the p-value from the simulations), `p_folded_sim` (the folded simulation p-value, as in PySAL), and `skewness` and `kurtosis` of the simulated values. `mean`, `median` and `pysal` give the quadrant, High-High, Low-Low, Low-High or High-Low. Unlike the global test, there is one value per county, so this shows where the clustering is, not just whether it exists.
:::

## Visualising Local Moran's I

`tm_polygons()` maps the `ii` field with fixed breaks.

::: panel-tabset
## The Plot

```{r}
#| echo: false
tmap_mode("plot")
tm_shape(lisa) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "ii",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "fixed",
                breaks = c(
                  -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5),
                values = "brewer.rd_bu"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "Local Moran's I")) +
                tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_view(set_zoom_limits = c(6,8)) +
  tm_title("local Moran's I of GDPPC") +
  tm_layout(legend.text.size = 1.2)
```

::: panel-tabset

# LISA Map

A LISA map is a categorical map of clusters and outliers. There are two types of outliers, High-Low and Low-High, and two types of clusters, High-High and Low-Low. It combines the local Moran's I of each county with its p-value.

## Plotting LISA Map

The `lisa` sf data frame has three fields with the LISA categories, `mean`, `median` and `pysal`. In general `mean` is used. `filter()` keeps only the counties whose simulated p-value is below 0.05, and those are drawn on top of a map of all 88 counties.

::: panel-tabset
## The Plot

```{r}
#| echo: false
lisa_sig <- lisa  %>%
  filter(p_ii_sim < 0.05)
tmap_mode("plot")
tm_shape(lisa) +
  tm_polygons() +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
tm_shape(lisa_sig) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "mean",
          fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(
            values = c("#0072B2", "#CC79A7", "#56B4E9", "#D55E00")),
          fill.legend = tm_legend(
            text.size = 1.15,
            width = 6)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.4) +
  tm_layout(legend.title.size = 1.25)
```

## The Code

```{r}
#| eval: false
lisa_sig <- lisa  %>%
  filter(p_ii_sim < 0.05)
tmap_mode("plot")
tm_shape(lisa) +
  tm_polygons() +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
tm_shape(lisa_sig) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "mean",
          fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(
            values = c("#0072B2", "#CC79A7", "#56B4E9", "#D55E00")),
          fill.legend = tm_legend(
            text.size = 1.15,
            width = 6)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.4) +
  tm_layout(legend.title.size = 1.25)
```
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning diary
`r nrow(lisa_sig)` counties are significant at 0.05. `r sum(lisa_sig$mean == "High-High")` of them are High-High, around Changsha in the north east. The colours follow the factor order Low-Low, High-Low, Low-High, High-High, so I set them in that order without green.
:::

# Hot Spot and Cold Spot Area Analysis (HCSA)

HCSA uses spatial weights to find statistically significant hot spots and cold spots, where similar high or low values sit close together. The features are usually administrative boundaries or a custom grid.

## Computing Local Gi* Statistics

As usual, a spatial weights matrix is needed first. `include_self()` adds each county to its own neighbour list, and `st_inverse_distance()` of **sfdep** weights each neighbour by one over its distance, so closer counties count more.

```{r}
wm_idw <- hunan_GDPPC %>%
  mutate(nb = include_self(
    st_contiguity(geometry)),
    wts = st_inverse_distance(nb,
                              geometry,
                              scale = 1,
                              alpha = 1),
         .before = 1)
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning diary
Gi* and local Gi* are distance-based statistics, so distance weights are used instead of contiguity weights. `include_self()` is needed because Gi* counts the county itself as part of its own neighbourhood.
:::

`local_gstar_perm()` computes Gi* for every county and tests each one with 99 simulations.

```{r}
set.seed(1234)
HCSA <- wm_idw %>%
  mutate(local_Gi = local_gstar_perm(
    GDPPC, nb, wts, nsim = 99),
         .before = 1) %>%
  unnest(local_Gi)
```

## Visualising Gi*

`tm_shape()` and `tm_fill()` of **tmap** map the local Gi* (`gi_star`) for each county.

::: panel-tabset

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning diary
`r nrow(HCSA_sig)` counties are significant at 0.05. The default palettes for the Gi* map and this map use green, so I set red for high and blue for low instead. `cluster` is ordered Low then High, so the colours go in that order. The hot spot areas around Changsha match the High-High cluster from local Moran's I above. The `cluster` field labels each county High or Low by its own GDPPC against the provincial mean, and `gi_star` gives the sign of the hot or cold spot. In Hands-on Exercise 5 I used the sign of `gi_star` to label hot and cold spots.
:::
